JUDGMENT AND REASONS
I. Background [1] The respondent is seeking to strike an application for judicial review filed by Lemay Co Inc, the applicant [Lemay or the applicant]. The applicant is applying for judicial review of the Minister of National Revenue’s [Minister] refusal to agree to increase the amount of the Canada Emergency Wage Subsidies [CEWS] the applicant considers it should receive for certain periods during which it was eligible.

[2] For the following reasons, the respondent failed to discharge his burden to show that the application for judicial review is doomed to fail, or that there is internal and effective recourse through which Lemay can advance its claim. For these reasons, the motion to strike is dismissed.
II. Facts [3] The parties are not challenging the following facts. During the COVID-19 pandemic, Lemay received the CEWS from August 2, 2020, to May 8, 2021, over 10 two-week pay periods; these periods bore numbers 6 to 15.

[4] After auditing the CEWS amounts Lemay received, the Minister noted that Lemay had made a calculation error and had claimed an amount greater than what it was eligible to receive for periods 6, 7 and 13 to 15, generating a $311,204 overpayment. Also, on account of the same calculation error, Lemay has claimed an amount lower than what it could have been eligible to receive for periods 8 to 12.

[5] On or around March 27, 2023, the Minister notified Lemay that she intended to assess it and to make adjustments for periods 6 to 7 and 13 to 15, namely, the periods for which Lemay had claimed more than it was eligible to receive.

[6] On May 12, 2023, Lemay asked the Minister to [translation] “apply her discretion” under subsection 125.7(16) of the Income Tax Act, RSC 1985, c 1 (5th Supp) [ITA] to increase the amount it could have claimed for periods 8 to 12. This change would have allowed Lemay to receive amounts greater than those it was paid at the time for these periods, for a total of $1,715,341.

[7] On June 22, 2023, the Minister confirmed that she intended to make an adjustment for periods 6, 7 and 13 to 15, but she refused Lemay’s application for periods 8 to 12, referring it to the Canada Revenue Agency’s [CRA] technical interpretation.

[8] On July 26, 2023, Lemay sent the Minister a new letter containing additional written submissions. Lemay asserted that under paragraph 164(1)(b) and subsection 152(3.4) of the ITA, the Minister may agree to grant CEWS amounts greater than those claimed in its original application for periods 8 to 12.

[9] In a September 11, 2023 letter, the Minister again refused as she did not have jurisdiction to allow Lemay’s claim. In the Minister’s opinion, it was not possible to make an upward adjustment for periods 8 to 12 (under paragraph 164(1)(b) and subsection 152(3.4)) because the amounts originally claimed had been paid; in addition, the amounts that were now being requested exceeded the amounts in the taxpayer’s initial claim, which had been filed within the prescribed time limits. Also, paragraph 125.7(5)(a) of the ITA limits the amount of the subsidy to the amount the taxpayer claimed in the first place. Lastly, the Minister cannot accept an amended application because, had Parliament so provided, [translation] “this power would have been conferred by the Act, as was done for original applications at subsection 125.7(16) of the ITA”.

[24] It should be noted that Lemay submitted that paragraph 164(1)(b) and subsection 152(3.4) of the ITA apply, an argument that the Minister rejected in her September 11, 2023 decision. These conclusions by the Minister are the subject of the application for judicial review.

[25] On this motion to strike, the respondent argues, in response to this argument, that subsection 152(3.4) aims to remedy the effects of paragraph 152(1)(b) and is not intended to allow entities to make upwards adjustments to original applications. According to the respondent, the purpose of subsection 152(3.4) of the ITA is to allow an eligible entity to obtain its subsidy immediately after the qualifying period by deeming the overpayment to have taken place at that time. Subsection 152(3.4) provides the following:
(3.4) The Minister may at any time determine the amount deemed by any of subsections 125.7(2) to (2.2) to be an overpayment on account of a taxpayer’s liability under this Part that arose during a qualifying period (as defined in subsection 125.7(1)), or determine that there is no such amount, and send a notice of the determination to the taxpayer.

JUDGMENT AND REASONS
I. Background [1] The respondent is seeking to strike an application for judicial review filed by Lemay Co Inc, the applicant [Lemay or the applicant]. The applicant is applying for judicial review of the Minister of National Revenue’s [Minister] refusal to agree to increase the amount of the Canada Emergency Wage Subsidies [CEWS] the applicant considers it should receive for certain periods during which it was eligible.

[2] For the following reasons, the respondent failed to discharge his burden to show that the application for judicial review is doomed to fail, or that there is internal and effective recourse through which Lemay can advance its claim. For these reasons, the motion to strike is dismissed.
II. Facts [3] The parties are not challenging the following facts. During the COVID-19 pandemic, Lemay received the CEWS from August 2, 2020, to May 8, 2021, over 10 two-week pay periods; these periods bore numbers 6 to 15.

[4] After auditing the CEWS amounts Lemay received, the Minister noted that Lemay had made a calculation error and had claimed an amount greater than what it was eligible to receive for periods 6, 7 and 13 to 15, generating a $311,204 overpayment. Also, on account of the same calculation error, Lemay has claimed an amount lower than what it could have been eligible to receive for periods 8 to 12.

[5] On or around March 27, 2023, the Minister notified Lemay that she intended to assess it and to make adjustments for periods 6 to 7 and 13 to 15, namely, the periods for which Lemay had claimed more than it was eligible to receive.

[6] On May 12, 2023, Lemay asked the Minister to [translation] “apply her discretion” under subsection 125.7(16) of the Income Tax Act, RSC 1985, c 1 (5th Supp) [ITA] to increase the amount it could have claimed for periods 8 to 12. This change would have allowed Lemay to receive amounts greater than those it was paid at the time for these periods, for a total of $1,715,341.

[7] On June 22, 2023, the Minister confirmed that she intended to make an adjustment for periods 6, 7 and 13 to 15, but she refused Lemay’s application for periods 8 to 12, referring it to the Canada Revenue Agency’s [CRA] technical interpretation.

[8] On July 26, 2023, Lemay sent the Minister a new letter containing additional written submissions. Lemay asserted that under paragraph 164(1)(b) and subsection 152(3.4) of the ITA, the Minister may agree to grant CEWS amounts greater than those claimed in its original application for periods 8 to 12.

[9] In a September 11, 2023 letter, the Minister again refused as she did not have jurisdiction to allow Lemay’s claim. In the Minister’s opinion, it was not possible to make an upward adjustment for periods 8 to 12 (under paragraph 164(1)(b) and subsection 152(3.4)) because the amounts originally claimed had been paid; in addition, the amounts that were now being requested exceeded the amounts in the taxpayer’s initial claim, which had been filed within the prescribed time limits. Also, paragraph 125.7(5)(a) of the ITA limits the amount of the subsidy to the amount the taxpayer claimed in the first place. Lastly, the Minister cannot accept an amended application because, had Parliament so provided, [translation] “this power would have been conferred by the Act, as was done for original applications at subsection 125.7(16) of the ITA”.
[10] On October 11, 2023, Lemay applied for judicial review of the decision.

[11] Despite the Minister’s decision concluding that she did not have the power to accept an amended application for an upward adjustment under subsection 125.7(16) of the ITA, on October 25, 2023, the respondent informally revised the position and suggested to Lemay that an analysis under subsection 125.7(16) of the ITA be conducted—contrary to the Minister’s decision of September 11, 2023—to determine whether the Minister could agree to grant the higher CEWS amounts claimed for periods 8 to 12.

[12] Lemay rejected this proposal given that it had already made such a request, which the Minister had refused in her September 11, 2023 letter. This letter remains the official, enforceable decision under judicial review before this Court.

[13] The respondent therefore brought this motion to strike, arguing that Lemay’s suggested interpretation of the relevant ITA provisions is doomed to fail and that, by reason of subsection 125.7(16) of the ITA, the application for judicial review is premature because Lemay has adequate internal and efficient recourse that it must exhaust before proceeding to judicial review.
III. Issue [14] The issue is whether the applicant’s application for judicial review is doomed to fail or premature on account of existing internal and efficient recourse.
IV. Analysis A. Applicable law [15] The Court may strike an application for judicial review that is doomed to fail or undertaken prematurely if there is internal and efficient recourse, in order to “restrain the misuse or abuse of courts’ processes” (Michaels of Canada, ULC v Canada (Attorney General), 2023 FCA 243; Canada (National Revenue) v JP Morgan Asset Management (Canada) Inc, 2013 FCA 250 at para 48 [JP Morgan]).

[16] However, an application for judicial review should not be struck out before a hearing on the merits is held, save for in exceptional cases such as when the notice of application is “so clearly improper as to be bereft of any possibility of success” (David Bull Laboratories (Canada) Inc v Pharmacia Inc (CA), [1995] 1 FC 588 at 600; JP Morgan at para 47; Lukács v Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada, 2015 FC 267 at para 21 [Lukács]).

[17] The party bringing the motion to strike a notice of application for judicial review must meet this stringent standard and demonstrate that it should be struck (Lukács at para 22; Benhsaien v Canada, 2024 FC 307 at paras 11–12; Canada v Preston, 2023 FCA 178 at para 16).

[18] When an application for judicial review raises a question of statutory interpretation, the Court’s role on a motion to strike is to determine whether the interpretation proposed by the applicant has a reasonable chance of success: “Once a judge finds that legislation is capable of being interpreted in at least two different ways, it is not open to the judge to conclude that it is plain and obvious that the action has no reasonable chance of success” (Mohr v National Hockey League, 2022 FCA 145 at para 47, see also paras 45–54 [Mohr]). In such cases, the motion to strike must be dismissed.

[19] The motions judge should therefore not make any definitive legal pronouncements on the meaning of legislation on a motion to strike where there are competing, credible interpretations on an honestly disputed point of statutory interpretation. In those cases, the Court must simply “determine whether there is a conflicting interpretation worth considering or that has a reasonable prospect of success” (Mohr at para 52).
B. The application for judicial review is not doomed to fail [20] Subsection 125.7(5) of the ITA provides the following:
(5) For the purposes of this section,
(a) the amount of any deemed overpayment by an eligible entity under any of subsections (2) to (2.2) in respect of a qualifying period cannot exceed the amount claimed by the eligible entity in the application referred to in paragraph (a) of the definition qualifying entity in subsection (1) — or paragraph (a) of the definition qualifying renter in subsection (1) or paragraph (a) of the definition qualifying recovery entity in subsection (1) — in respect of that qualifying period.
(5) Pour l’application du présent article, les règles ci-après s’appliquent :
a) le montant d’un paiement en trop déterminé en vertu des paragraphes (2) à (2.2) pour une période d’admissibilité d’une entité déterminée ne peut excéder le montant réclamé par l’entité dans la demande prévue à l’alinéa a) de la définition de entité admissible au paragraphe (1) — ou à l’alinéa a) de la définition de locataire admissible au paragraphe (1) ou à l’alinéa a) de la définition de entité de relance admissible au paragraphe (1) — relativement à cette période.

[21] The respondent submits that paragraph 125.7(5)(a) of the ITA prohibits the Minister from paying a subsidy amount greater than the amount initially claimed by a business. In his view, since the definition of [translation] “qualifying entity at subsection (1)” includes entities that file an application in respect of a given qualifying period as well as a specific amount that is claimed in prescribed form and based on a calculation set out in the ITA, paragraph 125.7(5)(a) clearly does not allow the Minister to grant an amount [translation] “exceeding” the amount claimed in said form. As a result, the language of paragraph 125.7(5)(a) is unambiguous and simply does not permit the Minister to pay the amount claimed; Lemay’s application is thus doomed to fail.

[22] According to Lemay, the issue does not end there. Subsection 125.7(5) of the ITA does not prevent a “qualifying entity” from amending an original CEWS application; it simply provides that the amount of any deemed overpayment by an eligible entity under subsection 125.7(2) of the ITA in respect of a qualifying period cannot exceed the amount claimed by the eligible entity. Lemay asserts that paragraph 125.7(5)(a) does not, however, address an entity’s right to file a new form to correct a calculation error in a previously submitted prescribed form.

[23] Lemay also claims that the Minister has an inherent power under the ITA to allow a new return by the taxpayer, in particular under subsection 152(3.4) and paragraph 164(1)(b) of the ITA. Consequently, the respondent’s argument does not completely respond to the application for judicial review, so in Lemay’s opinion, its application is not doomed to fail.

[24] It should be noted that Lemay submitted that paragraph 164(1)(b) and subsection 152(3.4) of the ITA apply, an argument that the Minister rejected in her September 11, 2023 decision. These conclusions by the Minister are the subject of the application for judicial review.

[25] On this motion to strike, the respondent argues, in response to this argument, that subsection 152(3.4) aims to remedy the effects of paragraph 152(1)(b) and is not intended to allow entities to make upwards adjustments to original applications. According to the respondent, the purpose of subsection 152(3.4) of the ITA is to allow an eligible entity to obtain its subsidy immediately after the qualifying period by deeming the overpayment to have taken place at that time. Subsection 152(3.4) provides the following:
(3.4) The Minister may at any time determine the amount deemed by any of subsections 125.7(2) to (2.2) to be an overpayment on account of a taxpayer’s liability under this Part that arose during a qualifying period (as defined in subsection 125.7(1)), or determine that there is no such amount, and send a notice of the determination to the taxpayer.
(3.4) Le ministre peut, à tout moment, déterminer le montant réputé par les paragraphes 125.7(2) à (2.2) être un paiement en trop qui se produit au cours d’une période d’admissibilité (au sens du paragraphe 125.7(1)), au titre des sommes dont le contribuable est redevable en vertu de la présente partie, ou déterminer qu’aucun tel montant n’existe et envoyer un avis de détermination au contribuable.
[26] In the respondent’s view, subsection 152(3.4) of the ITA therefore contains no ambiguity and remains subject to the limitation in subsection 125.7(5) of the ITA.

[27] However, the respondent made no argument rebutting Lemay’s position as regards the application of paragraph 164(1)(b) of the ITA. The respondent merely referred to subsection 152(4) of the ITA during his oral submissions, indicating that Lemay’s argument does not apply in this case. In my opinion, subsection 152(4) does not completely address Lemay’s argument on the application of subsection 152(3.4) and paragraph 164(1)(b) of the ITA. Most importantly, the respondent did not tackle whether, under subsections 152(3.4) and 125.7(5) and paragraph 164(1)(b) of the ITA, the Minister has an inherent power to allow an amendment to the prescribed form Lemay initially filed.

[28] In light of subsections 125.7(5) and 152(3.4) and paragraph 164(1)(b), which are the subject of this application for judicial review, it is therefore not clear, in considering these provisions together, that the ITA does not allow the Minister to admit an amended prescribed form, as the applicant is requesting. This issue is at the heart of the application for judicial review.

[29] On a motion to strike, it is not for this Court to determine the meaning of the ITA and to decide the issue of how to interpret the ITA provisions, insofar as there is more than one reasonable interpretation (Mohr at paras 45–52). That task is for the judge ruling on the merits of the application. In my view, it is not clear that subsections 125.7(5) and 152(3.4) and paragraph 164(1)(b) of the ITA, taken together, cannot allow for Lemay’s claim. Without full submissions regarding the context and purpose of these ITA provisions, I cannot, on a motion to strike, find that Lemay’s proposed interpretation has no reasonable chance of success.

[30] The respondent did not provide full and compelling submissions illustrating that subsections 152(3.4) and 125.7(5) and paragraph 164(1)(b) of the ITA, considered together, cannot be interpreted in the manner Lemay suggests—that is, that the Minister has the discretion to allow the filing of an amended prescribed form. As a result, the respondent did not meet his burden of demonstrating that it is plain and obvious that Lemay’s proposed interpretation has no reasonable chance of success, and so the application for judicial review is not clearly doomed to fail.
C. The application for judicial review is not premature [31] The respondent is asking the Court to strike out the application for judicial review on the ground that there is internal and effective recourse under subsection 125.7(16) of the ITA. Relying on paragraph 31 of the Federal Court of Appeal’s decision in Canada (Border Services Agency) v CB Powell Limited, 2010 FCA 61, the respondent argues that the Court may strike a premature application when an applicant has internal and effective recourse that could completely resolve the issue (see also JP Morgan at paras 84, 86).

[32] However, the facts in this case show that the Minister has already ruled on the recourse that the respondent is directing Lemay to seek: she has interpreted paragraph 125.7(16) in a narrow manner that does not allow Lemay to make its claim.

[33] Indeed, on May 12, 2023, Lemay first asked the Minister [translation] “to apply her discretion” under subsection 125.7(16) of the ITA to increase the amount it could have claimed for periods 8 to 12. On June 22, 2023, the Minister refused this claim, relying on the technical interpretation the CRA issued in document 2022-0941391I7(E), which is an internal administrative interpretation of the relevant ITA sections. In that document, the CRA indicates that subsection 125.7(16) does not affect the Minister’s ability to allow an application to amend a CEWS amount entered on a previous form.

[34] The Minister therefore determined that there is no recourse under subsection 125.7(16) and rejected the application that the respondent now claims is internal and effective recourse available to Lemay.

[35] Also, on September 11, 2023, when the CRA provided Lemay with the Minister’s decision to continue to refuse the application for increases respecting periods 8 to 12, it stated that subsection 125.7(16) provides that the CRA has the power to accept an original CEWS application, but not an amendment to an application that has already been presented.

[36] Today, the respondent submits to this Court that this is an error, and that there is indeed internal and effective recourse under subsection 125.7(16). Therefore, the respondent is essentially arguing that the Minister’s decision is unreasonable in terms of her interpretation of her own jurisdiction under subsection 125.7(16) of the ITA.

[37] Although the respondent’s interpretation as to the meaning of subsection 125.7(16) of the ITA is plausible, and potentially more aligned with the interpretation principle favouring such fair, large and liberal construction and interpretation as best ensures the attainment of its objects (Interpretation Act, RSC 1985, c I-21 at section 12), the fact remains that the Minister specifically rejected this interpretation in the decision that is the subject of the application for judicial review.

[38] As the Minister has already reached a conclusion and expressly rejected all internal recourse potentially available under subsection 125.7(16) of the ITA that could allow Lemay to file its application, there is no internal and effective recourse in this matter.

[39] In other words, the respondent cannot argue that there is internal and effective recourse under subsection 125.7(16) and that Lemay must follow this procedure, when the Minister has already rendered an enforceable decision to the contrary. It is open to the respondent to submit at the hearing on the merits that the Minister erred in this regard if the parties put this issue before the Court. However, as Lemay did not have internal recourse and as determined by the Minister, Lemay had to file an application for judicial review, which it did in this case.

[40] Allowing the respondent’s argument on the existence of internal and effective recourse under subsection 125.7(16) in this case would amount to ruling on the issue of whether the Minister’s decision was reasonable in terms of her interpretation of subsection 125.7(16) and her jurisdiction, in the absence of a debate and full submissions from the parties on this issue. However, this issue must be decided not by the judge disposing of a motion to strike, but by the trial judge if the issue is brought before him or her at the hearing on the application for judicial review.

[41] Consequently, on a motion to strike, the respondent cannot object to the Minister’s conclusions, ask the Court to ignore them, and order Lemay to submit an application that the Minister has already prohibited it from submitting.
V. Conclusion [42] The motion to strike is therefore dismissed.
